input.question: Why don't atoms in a molecule collapse each other's wavefunctions?
input.ground_truth: I think that some of the reason there is such confusion exhibited in the answers thus far is because this is related to a very much unresolved aspect of QM. We could say that, in response to your question, from the postulates of quantum mechanics measurement is the action of a Hermetian linear operator acting on a state vector which yields a real eigenvalue that corresponds to a physical observable. So two wavefunctions (the scalar product of the state vector and the real space position ket) overlapping or interacting doesn't represent such an act of measurement. There is no projection onto eigenstates. But that answer isn't really staisfying, since it just appeals to the postulates. So the best I can do beyond that is refer you to the (measurement problem)[_URL_0_] and point out that I also don't know how the (f & @k magnets work.)[_URL_1_]

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why don't atoms in a molecule collapse each other's wavefunctions?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine atoms are like little balls, and their wavefunctions are like the clouds that float around them. These clouds tell us where we might find the balls.

Now, when two balls (atoms) get close and make a team (a molecule), their clouds don’t just squish into one another. That’s because the balls don’t like to be in the same spot at the same time, kind of like how you don’t want to stand in the same spot as your friend at the same time on the playground.

So, their clouds (wavefunctions) mix together a little bit, but they don’t collapse into each other. They just change a little to make room for both balls to be happy and not bump into each other too much. That’s why the clouds don’t collapse into one big cloud—they stay separate but share a little space!
